books.section: Topic 6.10 Development of the Middle Class
Social Criticism in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text:
“The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.... The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. This change, however, is not to be deplored, but welcomed as highly beneficial.”

“The best means of benefiting the community is to place within its reach the ladders upon which the aspiring can rise — free libraries, parks, and means of recreation, by which men are helped in body and mind.... Thus is the problem of rich and poor to be solved. The laws of accumulation will be left free, the laws of distribution free. Individualism will continue, but the millionaire will be but a trustee for the poor.... Of such as these the public verdict will then be: ‘The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.’”

(Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889)
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889. Public domain; wording checked against the 1889 issue (archive.org scan) and the Norton Voices of Freedom reprint.

stem: Carnegie welcomes the contrast between “the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer” as “highly beneficial.” Social Darwinism defended inequality as natural. These two ideas could coexist in Gilded Age thought because

options.text: both accepted great fortunes and differed only on what the wealthy owed
both demanded the immediate breakup of all large corporations
options.misconception: Neither idea sought to break up corporations.

options.text: both were invented by labor unions to help workers
options.misconception: Both came from defenders of the industrial order, not from unions.

options.text: both argued that wealth should be distributed equally by the government to all
options.misconception: Neither called for government redistribution of wealth.

rationales.A: Carnegie welcomes great fortunes and adds a duty to give; Social Darwinism calls the same fortunes natural. Both start by accepting the fortunes.
rationales.B: Carnegie defends free accumulation. Social Darwinism defends competition. Neither wants corporations broken up.
rationales.C: Carnegie was a steel maker, and Social Darwinism came from defenders of business, not from labor unions.
rationales.D: Carnegie leaves the laws of accumulation and distribution free. Neither idea hands wealth to the government.
rationales.general:
Find what the two ideas share before you list how they differ.
1. Carnegie welcomes the millionaire's palace as highly beneficial.
2. Background from the books: Social Darwinism called inequality natural, the survival of the fittest in business.
3. Both therefore treat great fortunes as legitimate.
4. They differ only on the next step: Carnegie adds a duty to give back.
Remember: two ideas can coexist when they share a premise and differ on a conclusion.
